name: Nose contouring makeup
lead: Nose contouring is a makeup technique in which a darker shade is applied along the sides of the nose and a lighter shade on the bridge or tip, with the aim of making the nose look slimmer, straighter, shorter or more defined through light and shadow. It is a specific application of contouring, defined as using cosmetics to define, enhance and sculpt facial structure [1].

The look rests on a simple optical principle: darker shades create shadow and make an area recede, while lighter shades bring forward areas that are more prominent [1][2]. Makeup artists describe fitting the placement to the nose: for example, Wayne Goss suggests different placements for flat, triangular, crooked, bulbous and narrow noses, and makeup artist Allie Smith demonstrated a version meant to widen a narrow nose [2][3].

The effect lasts as long as the makeup is worn and washes off at the end of the day. It does not change the structure of the nose. It is widely discussed alongside non-surgical options such as hyaluronic acid filler and surgical rhinoplasty as the lowest-commitment way to change how the nose looks, and is used in everyday makeup, photography and stage, film and drag makeup [1][4]. No published study has measured its effect on perceived nose shape.

paras: In general contouring, a shade one or two tones darker than the skin is placed in hollows such as along the sides of the nose, cheeks and temples to create shadow, and a lighter shade is placed on more prominent areas to draw light [1]. Powder palettes with light and dark shades and cream products are commonly used [1]. Strobing is a related approach that uses lighter shades only [1].

Powder contour gives a softer result, while cream contour can give a more emphasised look [1]. Into The Gloss advises choosing the formula by skin type: creams suit dry skin, while powders, matte products or dry pencils suit oily skin, and it notes that ordinary eyeshadow, brow pencil, bronzer or concealer can stand in for dedicated contour products [3].

Makeup artists describe a common sequence: foundation or concealer first, a darker shade drawn in two lines down either side of the bridge, a lighter shade down the centre and sometimes on the tip, then blending until no hard edge remains [3][5]. Charlotte Tilbury's guide describes a thin line of darker concealer-style product down the bridge and a dot on the tip for slight lift, with contour on each side, and calls blending the most important step for a subtle result [5].

Placement is varied to alter the perceived shape. In Wayne Goss's guide at Beautylish, a flat nose gets two straight contour lines along the bridge; a triangular nose gets contour only on the tip; a crooked nose gets straight lines on both sides with highlight down the centre to straighten it; a bulbous nose gets contour on the very top and bottom with highlight on the bridge; a narrow nose gets highlight lines along the sides to add thickness; and a heavy brow that shadows the bridge gets highlight between the brows [2]. Lines placed closer together than the actual bridge are described as suggesting a narrower, higher bridge, while lines set wider and stopping at the nostrils are described as suggesting a wider nose [3].

Shading the face with makeup has theatrical roots: Elizabethan stage actors reportedly used chalk and soot, and greasepaint replaced soot after electric stage lighting arrived in the late 1800s [1]. Film actress Marlene Dietrich is reported to have contoured her own face in the 1920s and 1930s [1]. Max Factor Sr. added shading to film makeup in 1934 so faces would not look flat on screen, and presented a contouring tutorial for different face shapes in 1945 [1]. Actresses of the 1950s such as Audrey Hepburn, Marilyn Monroe and Elizabeth Taylor wore subtle contouring [1].

Makeup artist Kevyn Aucoin's 2000 book Face Forward is credited with introducing contouring to the general public, and celebrities such as Kim Kardashian are credited with popularising it further in the 2010s as affordable brands began selling dedicated contour and strobing products [1]. Drag performers use contouring to emphasise or soften features [1].

Appearance communities often compare nose contouring with non-surgical rhinoplasty using hyaluronic acid filler, a technique described in a 2025 Indian Journal of Plastic Surgery article, and with surgical rhinoplasty [4]. Contouring is the only one of these that is fully removable at the end of the day.

Within appearance communities, nose contouring is generally described as a reversible, non-surgical way to alter perceived nose width or straightness, often for photos or events. Brand and artist guides present it as a technique anyone can learn with ordinary products [2][3][5].
Risks are those of ordinary cosmetics, such as irritation or breakouts in sensitive skin. Cream products are noted by artists as more likely to smudge on oily skin [3].
No studies found. Published research that appears in searches for related terms concerns surgical nasal reconstruction and nasal anatomy rather than the effect of makeup on perceived nose shape.

lore.intro: Nose contouring is mostly described by makeup artists and brands rather than in forums; their claims are about what light and shadow do to the perceived shape.

claims.claim: Dark shade on the sides and light down the middle makes a nose look slimmer
claims.believers: Artists say shadow makes the sides recede while highlight brings the bridge forward [1][2].
claims.experts: No published study has tested the effect on perceived nose shape.

claims.claim: Placement should be matched to nose shape
claims.believers: Wayne Goss describes different placements for flat, triangular, crooked, bulbous and narrow noses [2].
claims.experts: No studies have compared placement approaches.

claims.claim: Blending is what separates a natural look from a visible stripe
claims.believers: Charlotte Tilbury's guide calls blending the key to a subtle result [5].
claims.experts: No research on this; it is professional technique advice.

claims.claim: A narrow nose can be made to look wider
claims.believers: Allie Smith's demonstration shows darker lines on the sides with a lighter shade between them to widen a narrow nose [3].
claims.experts: No published study has examined this.

card.summary: Shading and highlighting to make the nose look slimmer; purely optical, reversible and untested in studies.
card.note: Temporary visual effect only; no studies of its perceived effect were found.

quick.overview:
Nose contouring uses a darker shade on the sides of the nose and a lighter one on the bridge or tip to create the illusion of a slimmer, straighter nose.
It is an established makeup technique with roots in theatre and film, popularized more widely in the 2010s.
quick.mechanism: Dark shades recede and light shades advance visually, so shading along the sides of the nose can make it look narrower. Nothing about the underlying structure changes.
quick.risks: Risks are those of ordinary cosmetics, such as skin irritation or breakouts in sensitive individuals. The effect disappears when the makeup is removed.

chain: Darker shade applied along sides of the nose
Lighter shade placed on bridge or tip
Shadow and highlight change how light reads on the nose
Nose appears slimmer and straighter while worn
angle.text: Nose contouring changes the look of the nose right away with powder or cream makeup and washes off at the end of the day. People use it for events, photos and everyday makeup when they want a slimmer or straighter-looking nose without any procedure.
